item.itunes:title: 50歲後你該這樣練，五日膝蓋居家訓練運動！！
item.itunes:author: 三個字SunGuts
item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Kw-BmbDU4U

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解長輩膝蓋退化與不願出門背後的活動量過低與肌力流失惡性循環。
  • 學習五個在家即可安全施作的下肢肌力與平衡訓練動作，有效減輕膝蓋負擔。
  • 掌握長輩起坐困難的環境因素，了解合適的家具高度與坐姿支撐對關節保護的重要性。

摘要

破解活動量與肌力流失的惡性循環

宋物理治療師指出，許多長輩隨著年齡增長而變得無法或不願外出散步，往往被歸咎於膝蓋自然老化，但主要肇因其實是日常負重與活動刺激不足。當腿部肌肉量與耐力大幅衰退，日常活動變得吃力，便會形成「越累越想坐、越不動越無力」的惡性循環。為此，作者強調保護膝蓋必須從臀部控制與下肢肌力著手，並提供了一套能在家中執行的循序漸進鍛鍊計畫。

強化髖關節與股四頭肌：蚌殼式與靠牆深蹲

第一項訓練是蚌殼式，目標在於加強行走單腳承重時維持骨盆與大腿穩定的臀部肌群；操作時側躺屈膝、雙腳疊放，穩定控制上側膝蓋如蚌殼般開合，左右各做十次、進行三組。第二項則是靠牆深蹲，專門改善長輩因股四頭肌無力而起身困難的問題。背貼牆面、雙腳踩穩微往前，順著牆面緩慢微蹲並維持五秒再站起，重複十次為一組，可依能力逐步增加維持時間或下蹲深度，過程中須避免膝關節產生疼痛與內夾。

平衡腿部肌力：扶椅勾腿與輔助分腿蹲

第三項運動是扶椅勾腿，補足一般居家運動較少訓練到的大腿後側膕繩肌；雙手扶穩固定椅背，單腳將腳跟朝臀部勾起後緩慢下放，若覺得輕鬆亦可配合彈力帶增加阻力，單側進行十五次。第四項為輔助分腿蹲，採前後分腿姿勢，雙手扶椅輔助，雙膝微彎微幅下蹲，藉由前腳的大腿與臀部主導發力，單側重複十次並交替進行三組，能有效增強跨步時所需的單側承重與控制力。

提升側向步態穩定與日常起坐環境改善

最後一項是側向跨步練習，雙手扶著穩固表面並徹底移轉身體重心橫向邁步，切忌拖地或雙腳交叉，此動作有助於提升閃避障礙與側移時的平衡感。針對缺乏運動習慣的長者，作者建議每週安排兩至三天，每次挑選一到兩個動作漸進執行。此外，久坐低矮柔軟的沙發也是造成起身吃力的主因，作者建議看電視進廣告時應起身走動，並介紹了具備較高座高、淺座深與扎實支撐的工學沙發設計，幫助肌力較弱的長輩能更安全、輕鬆地起立與休息。

================================================

Hi everyone, I’m physical therapist Song . Are your elderly family members increasingly unwilling to go out for a walk, or are they increasingly unable to ? Many people think that as you age, your knees just naturally get worse, but a big part of this is actually related to how little you move every day. When your body stops being exposed to the weight-bearing demands of standing or walking for long periods, your leg muscles and overall stamina will drop significantly. Things you could once do start to become difficult, so you move even less. This creates a cycle: the more tired you feel, the more you want to sit and rest, and the less you move,. the more you lose your original strength . So, in today's video, I want to show you how to train and regain the strength in the muscles around your knees and the control needed to stand up and move, all from home. The first exercise we can do is the " clamshell," which targets the hips. Because when we walk and shift our weight to one leg, our hip muscles control the pelvis and thigh position. Since thigh control affects how your knees move, protecting your knees must start with your hips. For this movement, start by lying on.

your side on a flat surface. You can place a pillow under your head. Bend both knees slightly forward and stack your feet together. Place your top hand in front of your pelvis to ensure your body doesn't rotate while moving. Next, keep your heels together and slowly open your top knee, then close it again, just like a clamshell opening and shutting. With this movement, we are training our hip strength. The key is to open it steadily for a short distance, then slowly bring it back. The focus is to feel the hip of your top leg working and engaging. Once. finished, flip over and repeat on the other side. I recommend ten repetitions per side, alternating sides to complete one set, and doing this for a total of three sets. The second exercise we’ll train is the wall squat, because many seniors need to use their hands for support when standing up. This is usually because their quadriceps are too weak to stand up on their own. Therefore, we can use this method to strengthen them. First, stand with your back against the wall, feet about hip-width apart. Step your feet slightly forward so your soles are firmly planted.

, and ensure the floor is non-slip. Next , slide your back slowly down the wall. As you move, squat down a little bit; once you feel your thighs starting to engage, just hold it there. Once you're in this position, breathe normally, hold for five seconds, and then slowly stand back up. You don't need to squat until your thighs are parallel to the floor right away. If you haven't exercised for a long time, it’s okay if a shallow squat feels difficult; just squat to that height. During the process, keep your knees pointing in the same direction as your toes, and keep your feet firmly planted. If you feel any. significant pain in your knees during the exercise, move back up to a higher position. Once this depth feels too easy , you can slowly increase the holding time or squat a little bit lower. Each squat, holding for five seconds and then standing back up, counts as one repetition. We suggest doing 10 reps per set, resting, and repeating this for three sets. The third exercise is the chair-supported leg curl, because many lower-limb exercises only involve raising the leg while seated, so the back of the thighs is rarely trained independently. When performing this, stand in front of a sturdy chair back and hold on with both hands. Make sure.

the chair is fixed and won't slide. If it’s too slippery, you can use a fixed countertop instead. To start, shift your center of gravity onto your left leg. Keep your right thigh roughly in its original position. Then, slowly bend your knee to lift your heel toward your glutes, making sure to lower it back down slowly. You don't need to have your heels touch your glutes during this movement; just bend as far as you comfortably can. Ensure you feel the tension in your hamstrings throughout the motion, and keep control as you lower your leg, rather than letting it drop. After we finish one side, we’ll move on to the. other. If you find doing this with just your body weight too easy, you can add a resistance band to increase the challenge. To train your right leg, loop one end of the band around your right ankle and step on the other end with your foot. Make sure the band is secure, use your hands for support, and begin the leg curl. The movement is the same: keep your thigh in place and slowly lift your right heel toward your glutes. When lowering, maintain even more control; don't just relax and let the band snap your leg back. I recommend performing 15 repetitions per side; alternating both.

sides counts as one set. For the next exercise, I suggest doing a supported split squat to help strengthen your glutes and thighs. Usually, when we take a stride, our feet are positioned one in front of the other . For this movement, we will use a chair . Stand next to a sturdy, non-slip chair ; if you don't have a good chair, a table will work, too. Starting with the right foot forward and the left foot back, take a step forward with your right foot, keeping your feet wider than your hip width. Make sure your front right foot is. firmly planted. It's fine for your back left heel to be lifted, as it only needs to support you on the ball of your foot. Before we start the movement, make sure you are standing in a stable position. Then, slowly bend both knees together to lower your body a short distance, and then slowly rise back up. The main focus is to have your front foot drive the movement, with your back foot simply providing balance and support. Done. Returning to the standing height, ensure your front heel stays planted throughout the process, and keep your knee tracking in the direction of your toes, avoiding any inward collapse. The key is to feel.

both the thigh and the hip of your front leg working at the same time. So, to start, we don't need to squat too deep, and you don't need to let your back knee touch the floor. You don't have to go that low; just feel the front of your thigh engaging. If you find it difficult, you can make the movement smaller or use your hands for more support to help out a bit more . Once you can perform each repetition steadily on the way down and back up, we can gradually increase the depth of your squat. I suggest doing ten repetitions of this single-leg squat, alternating between sides to complete one set, and. we can repeat this for three sets. For the final exercise, we will practice side-stepping. This movement is useful when walking with someone and you need to shift to the side or step aside to let someone pass. First, stand by a stable surface, hold on with both hands , and make sure there are no obstacles nearby. Next, take a small step to the right with your right foot, shift your body over, and let your left foot follow . Once you've reached the end, stand steady, then switch to stepping to the left with your left foot, shift your body, and bring your right foot to catch up, moving back and forth like this.

Remember, as you step out, your body must move with it so that the leg truly bears the weight, allowing the other leg to come over. Start with smaller, slower steps, but make sure to lift your feet completely; never drag them on the floor , and avoid crossing your legs or tripping over yourself. You can keep holding on with your hands, and once your side-to-side movement feels stable , you can gradually reduce the support from your hands. These five exercises are recommended for seniors at home who need knee care or haven't exercised in a long time. If your elderly family members have almost no exercise routine, how should. they get started with these five movements? I suggest picking just one or two movements they can manage first; there is no need to do them all in one day, and we can gradually add more over time. We can schedule workouts weekly, aiming for two to three sessions if possible. The key is that if your knees get increasingly painful during exercise , or if they swell up afterward, it means there is an issue with how you're training, perhaps the movements themselves, or your knees might have severe inflammation and require treatment or a professional assessment. Additionally, many seniors experience this because they spend hours sitting on.

the sofa watching TV without moving, sometimes even falling asleep while doing so. So, I suggest that whenever you see a commercial or finish a segment of a show , you should stand up and walk around for a bit to give your legs a chance to move. When standing up from the sofa, you might also notice if your sofa is too deep, making it difficult to stand up and forcing you to use your hands to push yourself up. For seniors with less leg strength, a sofa that is too low and too soft makes just standing up very strenuous, and even dangerous. That is why I’d like to introduce the "Ultimate. Ergonomic Sofa" from my own brand. When designing it, I took both comfortable seating and ease of standing into consideration. Our entire sofa is made a bit higher, much higher than a standard sofa, but the surface of the cushion retains a soft feel while the base provides sufficient support. Furthermore, we made the seat depth shallower so that when your back rests against the backrest, your feet can still touch the floor. If your legs are shorter, you can use the adjustable footrest to support your feet according to your needs. This allows the seniors in your home, or even you, to find a.

comfortable position while watching TV or chatting with family. So, if you are interested in this " Ultimate Ergonomic Sofa," or if your seniors at home have similar issues and need a suitable chair, you can click the link below to fill out the sofa usage survey. Once completed, you can receive an early-bird discount for when the product launches. My main hope is that everyone can rest comfortably at home and maintain the ability to stand up and go out whenever you want to. I am Three Words.

第一項訓練是蚌殼式，目標在於加強行走單腳承重時維持骨盆與大腿穩定的臀部肌群；操作時側躺屈膝、雙腳疊放，穩定控制上側膝蓋如蚌殼般開合，左右各做十次、進行三組。第二項則是靠牆深蹲，專門改善長輩因股四頭肌無力而起身困難的問題。背貼牆面、雙腳踩穩微往前，順著牆面緩慢微蹲並維持五秒再站起，重複十次為一組，可依能力逐步增加維持時間或下蹲深度，過程中須避免膝關節產生疼痛與內夾。

平衡腿部肌力：扶椅勾腿與輔助分腿蹲

第三項運動是扶椅勾腿，補足一般居家運動較少訓練到的大腿後側膕繩肌；雙手扶穩固定椅背，單腳將腳跟朝臀部勾起後緩慢下放，若覺得輕鬆亦可配合彈力帶增加阻力，單側進行十五次。第四項為輔助分腿蹲，採前後分腿姿勢，雙手扶椅輔助，雙膝微彎微幅下蹲，藉由前腳的大腿與臀部主導發力，單側重複十次並交替進行三組，能有效增強跨步時所需的單側承重與控制力。
